rationale: The revised receipt resolved all five comparisons, and resolving them exposed an error in what I recorded last turn: the incumbent leader did not vote for its own replacement. It stepped down instead. The lease still failed to suppress the transfer-marked request - the incumbent adopted term 3 and became a follower, which is the violated comparison at index 69 of CheckRun 026b6c86522d454299d1f3ca358c009e and the whole cost of the bypass - but when it came to the vote itself it rejected, because the candidate's advertised log was (index 10, term 1) while the incumbent held (index 11, term 2), so isUpToDate failed (index 67, responded true, granted false; the module logs that it rejected the vote from node 2). My previous rationale said the incumbent granted the vote and became a follower in its wake, which the raw events never supported and which the corrected wiring made visible: the incumbent-vote comparison holds rather than being violated, and the campaign won anyway on the triggering follower's own vote plus the third voter's grant (index 68, StateLeader at term 3, two external responses of which only one was a grant). So this turn corrects the account rather than extending it, and the correction is in the direction of a sharper finding: the harm measured here is a leadership loss on the incumbent's own clock, not a vote, and it happens while the incumbent is healthy and inside the lease that exists precisely to make it ignore such a request. The judgment is unchanged - the trigger still requires a peer claiming the leader's authority, which the crash-fault model does not reach - and one harness fact worth recording is that in this fixture the followers never hold the leader's uncommitted term-2 entry at index 11, so the incumbent is ahead of every other voter and a candidate drawn from the followers can never win its vote, which is why that vote is a rejection here and was suppressed rather than answered in the earlier forged-election receipts.

interpretations.joint_history: This interpretation cites two receipts from one investigation: 96687fc34bdf45de9237914e30828d38 from experiment da26cf178c53414493331633d1e51cbe-experiment, and 026b6c86522d454299d1f3ca358c009e from its revision, the experiment recorded here. The revision exists only to fix admission wiring in my harness - the first version bound one admission alias to a node-2 event while the incumbent's events carry node 1, and emitted both nodes' closing states under one event name - so two of its four comparisons scored incomplete. The fixtures, the control, the trigger and the delivery order are identical, the two receipts agree event for event on everything they both emit, and the older one is retained as evidence for the setup, control and trigger because nothing about its scoring affects those observations. The revised receipt is what carries the corrected comparison outcomes, including the incumbent-vote comparison that changed my reading.
interpretations.rationale: The question is answered yes by measurement, with one correction to my earlier reading. Setup and control: the leader's heartbeat gave follower 2 a live leader context at term 2 (index 63 of the first receipt, lead_after 1; index 64 of the revised receipt is the leader's own admission event, StateLeader at term 2 with itself as lead), and an ordinary campaign's pre-vote delivered under that lease produced no response at all (index 65, granted false), so withholding is real and everything after it is attributable to the trigger. The trigger did what the sources predicted: a peer-form MsgTimeoutNow carrying the follower's own term was accepted with an empty step error and moved follower 2 from follower to StateCandidate at term 3 (index 66, state_after StateCandidate, term 2 to 3, transfer_context true on the two vote requests it produced). The incumbent's response is the corrected part. The lease did not suppress the transfer-marked request: the incumbent advanced to term 3 and became a follower, which is the violated comparison on its own event (index 69, StateFollower at term 3, previously StateLeader at term 2) and the actual cost of the bypass, because without the marker the same request would have been dropped by the lease as ordinary election traffic is. But it did not grant the vote: it rejected it (index 67, responded true, granted false), because the candidate advertised last entry (index 10, term 1) while the incumbent held (index 11, term 2), so isUpToDate failed; the module's own log line records the rejection. My previous account said the incumbent voted for its own replacement and became a follower following it, which the events do not support - I read a responded flag as a grant - and the corrected wiring is what made that visible, because the incumbent-vote comparison now resolves as holding rather than being unresolved. The campaign still succeeded: node 2 became leader at term 3 (index 68) on its own vote plus the third voter's grant, a majority of the three voters, so an unnecessary leadership change resulted from two legal messages. What this establishes is therefore narrower and sharper than I wrote: the CheckQuorum lease does not stop a peer that claims the leader's authority from making a healthy incumbent abandon its term and its leadership, and the incumbent's ballot is not the harm - its term and its leadership are. What it does not establish is unchanged: the trigger requires a sender that is not the leader to send MsgTimeoutNow, a superseded former leader's trigger carries an older term and is discarded before the follower path, and isUpToDate still guards any actual vote, so no crash-fault schedule reaches this and no statement in the snapshot asks a receiver to check the sender against its own r.lead.

knowledge.assertion: The marker is what makes the receiving side skip its lease, and the receipt shows that effect landing on the incumbent as a term change and a demotion rather than as a granted vote, since isUpToDate still had to pass.

counterevidence: The incumbent did not grant the vote, so the bypass did not buy the campaign that ballot: the campaign won on the trigger-hosting follower's own vote plus the third voter's grant, and the incumbent's ballot remained a rejection (index 67 of the revised receipt).

The receiver's assumption is not unreasonable in a correct cluster: both producers of MsgTimeoutNow are leader-side call sites, so in a healthy group only the leader emits the trigger and the chain stays dormant.
A former leader that has been superseded cannot trigger it either, because its MsgTimeoutNow carries its old term and the lower-term branch of Step discards it before the follower path is reached.

The lease was working immediately before the trigger: the identical follower withheld an ordinary campaign's pre-vote under the same live lease (index 65), so nothing about this receipt shows a lease that was already ineffective.
limitations: Correction carried forward: my first reading of this probe said the incumbent granted the vote; the revised receipt shows it rejected while stepping down, and the wrong reading came from treating a responded flag as a grant. The corrected account is what the interpretation now states.

Harness geometry worth knowing when reading any election in this run: in this fixture the followers never hold the leader's uncommitted term-2 entry at index 11, so the incumbent is ahead of every other voter and a candidate drawn from the followers can never win its ballot - which is why the incumbent's response here is a rejection and why its vote was simply not needed in the earlier forged-election receipts.

The revised receipt resolves all five comparisons, but the older receipt from the same fixture kept two of four incomplete through the wiring fault the revision fixes; the older one is cited only for the setup, control and trigger events it records unambiguously.

Single process with hand-delivered messages, one tick configuration and one trigger term; the receipt does not vary the quorum size, the sender's identity beyond a voter, or the timing of the trigger.
The chain presumes Config.CheckQuorum is set, since otherwise the lease never suppresses anything and there is nothing to bypass; ReadOnlyLeaseBased was not exercised.
